title: Galilee of the nations (Matthew 4:12–25)
hook: a great light for a people sitting in darkness, by the sea road
tomorrow: who reaches him first when he comes down the mountain?

segments.voice: Yesterday, three tests in the wilderness, three answers from Deuteronomy, and a tempter who quoted a psalm. Your line: it is written.

Every town has a road where the streetlights go out first and get fixed last. Nobody holds a launch party there, and nobody posts the photos. So where does a light start? John the Baptist has been thrown into prison, and Jesus doesn't head for Jerusalem, the city of the temple. He leaves Nazareth and settles in Capernaum, a town "upon the sea coast," a place of boats and nets.
screen: `THE STREETLIGHT FIXED LAST.` → `NOT JERUSALEM.` → `CAPERNAUM, BY THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Matthew hears the prophet Isaiah in that move: "Galilee of the Gentiles; The people which sat in darkness saw great light." In Isaiah's own chapter, the King James says Galilee of the nations: the peoples beyond Israel. Isaiah's words belong first to the Hebrew Bible, which Jews read as their own scripture. Then Jesus begins to preach, "Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand," and calls two fishermen at their nets: "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." So the answer to today's question: in Matthew, the light starts on a shoreline, among working people, in a place a prophet called the shadow of death. Light is shared ground with a neighbor. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth." Muslims and Christians both reach for light to speak of God reaching people in the dark. And one honest difference: Matthew sees the light dawn in a person, Jesus, who in John's Gospel says, "I am the light of the world." In the Qur'an, the Light is God's alone, and Jesus is honored as a messenger of God. Two traditions, one image, each in its own words.
screen: `DARKNESS SAW GREAT LIGHT.` · `FISHERS OF MEN.` · `THE QUR'AN: ALLAH IS THE LIGHT.` · `ONE IMAGE, TWO MEANINGS.` · then, large: `LIGHT BY THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Turn on one lamp, or face the brightest window, and look at the light for a few breaths. Then let one neglected place come to mind, a street, a care home, a neighbor's door, a corner of your own life left dark, and hold the light and that place together until the sit ends.
Galilee of the nations. Isaiah's name for the land by the sea where, Matthew says, a people in darkness saw great light.
Here's your line: light by the sea, and in Matthew it starts among the fishing boats. Until tomorrow.

notes: Matthew 4:15 (KJV) reads 'Galilee of the Gentiles'; Isaiah 9:1 (KJV) reads 'Galilee of the nations'. The voice calls them 'two English words for the same idea'; the underlying Greek of Matthew is ta ethne. Confirm the wording.
'His first words are nearly word for word John's': Matthew 3:2 'Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand' vs 4:17 'Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.'
No claim is made about Galilee's population or how mixed it was; 'two old tribal lands' refers to Zebulun and Naphtali, which Matthew names.
The calling of the fishermen is told briefly here, without 'straightway' (4:20, 4:22), so as not to anticipate day 1436's 'follow now'.
'The city of the temple and the powerful' describes Jerusalem in general terms; confirm.
howItsDone: Isaiah 9 at Christmas and Matthew 4 after Epiphany are hedged as 'some'; confirm.
